description: I'm Walubo Nathan, a computer scientist in Kampala. Our team is building a simple, reliable health monitoring tool for astronauts that tracks vital signs and flags early risks. Join us if you want a collaborative team focused on a working prototype and strong pitch. Need: ML/data, UI/UX, health or space expertise.
summary:
What we developed. Astro-Doctor is a wellbeing platform for astronauts on long space missions, built around adaptive virtual reality (VR). A 90-second daily check-in on mood, sleep, energy and alertness, plus the mission phase, selects a VR world and a 10–30 minute session. Astronauts design their own family avatars, home and hometown, relatives send typed notes into the scenes, and games link to the station's exercise machines.
How it addresses the challenge. Mood and coping hit their lowest in the third quarter of a mission, yet support stays flat. Astro-Doctor monitors mood and sleep every day, raises support through that dip, and alerts flight surgeons, with the astronaut's consent, if low mood persists.
Why it is important. A Mars round trip lasts over two years, and NASA expects behavioral risk to rise with distance from Earth. VR already flies on the ISS, and the same approach can support Antarctic crews, hospital patients, migrant workers and elders in care.

What it does and how it works. Astro-Doctor runs a daily 90-second check-in on mood, sleep and energy, then uses it and the mission phase to pick a VR world and session length, adding more support in the third quarter.

Benefits. Support rises when morale dips, keeps astronauts connected to home, encourages exercise and warns flight surgeons early.

Intended impact. Less depression, sleep trouble and isolation on long missions such as Mars, and support for others far from home.

Tools used. A web portal with check-ins and VR scene recommendations, VR headsets and station exercise machines. Team to confirm: languages, frameworks and VR engine.

How it is creative. Support follows the predicted morale dip, with personal avatars, typed family notes and exercise as play.

Factors we considered. Timing of risk, personalisation, consent and ethics, session limits, and supporting rather than replacing medical staff.
